catalog_quote: Descriptively, we may say that in Michif words of three syllables or fewer, primary stress falls on the final syllable and secondary stress surfaces in three syllable words on the first syllable, while in words of four syllables or more, primary stress falls on the antepenult and secondary stress is alternating throughout the word. Note that this pattern holds regardless of the language source of the word in question: historically Cree (data in 1-5, a, b) and historically French (data in 1-3, c,d) lexical items, as well as items of mixed origin (data in 4c-d, 5c, 6a) pattern in the same way. ... First of all, Michif stress may be characterized as consisting of bounded iambs, from the right edge. ... in words of three syllables or less stress is word-final while in words of more than three syllables it is on the antepenult. ... (12) Michif parameter settings: (i) bounded feet yes, binary…
sweep_summary: One works with stress in the title only: Rosen (2006) 'Language contact and Michif stress assignment', STUF 59(2):170-190, already in the per-language bibliography. It is squarely about Michif word stress but the full text is paywalled at De Gruyter (live page returns an AWS WAF challenge; Semantic Scholar marks it CLOSED; CORE, the Internet Archive PDF and academia/scholar lookups gave nothing; The abstract, recovered from a 2024 Internet Archive copy of the De Gruyter page and, says the paper offers a first analysis of Michif word stress, derives the system from both Plains Cree and French, and finds Cree- and French-source words pattern alike - consistent with the catalog's classification but without naming the stressed syllable. The catalog's deciding source, Rosen's 2007 Toronto dissertation (Chapter 7 'Michif Stress', p. 221), is held by the project and the PDF), cites the 2006 article, and gives the full statement (final primary stress in words of three syllables or fewer, antepenultimate in four or more, regardless of source); the 2006 article is the earlier journal version of that analysis, so acquiring it is low priority - it would at most refine, not replace, the dissertation. No new first-hand statement was read in this search of works with stress in the title; the catalog's 'fixed-unreviewed' entry with the Rosen 2007 quote stands.

sources.quote: This paper examines stress assignment in Michif, a contact language with its roots in French and Plains Cree ... First, to propose a first analysis of word stress in Michif, and second, to compare Michif word stress with Plains Cree and French word stress assignment systems ... I show that the Michif stress system derives from both the Plains Cree and French stress systems ... the new system is distinct from either, as lexical items from both Plains Cree and French vocabularies pattern in the same way. This is evidence against the commonly held view that Michif displays a split phonology based on language source (BAKKER 1997, BAKKER & PAPEN 1997, PAPEN 2003).
